lessons.text: The first charter draft named the fix ('install a second machine head') instead of the problem, and the prescore's solution-language flag forced the rewrite. That failure was load-bearing: the matrix later scored the second head last on cost and effort, and the $40 method change it would have pre-empted recovered 64.8% of the gap. Write the problem, not the remedy -- the tool that caught it earned its place.

We spent our one pre-declared Analyze comparison on the daypart split expecting a staffing story, and it came back real but minor (0.45 min, d = -0.44) -- a dead end as a driver. The dead end paid for itself: it kept the project off a schedule reshuffle that could not have recovered more than a fraction of a 3.4-minute gap, and it kept the staffing cause honestly labeled 'investigating' instead of verified.

Meeting the mean goal is not the every-order promise. The improved process is stable at 4.90 minutes -- and with sd 0.65 against the 5.0 line, Cpk is 0.05 and the model puts ~43.9% of orders over five minutes. Saying so plainly at close is what keeps the next project honest: the center moved; the spread is the remaining work.

provenance.method: gap = |goal - baseline| directionally; recovered = |after - baseline| directionally; remaining = gap - recovered; goal_met = remaining <= 0 (PLAN §4.1 Improve-loop gap arithmetic, rubric R-IMP-04, BoK IV.C.1)

panels.narrative: Espresso orders at the campus coffee bar were taking too long during the weekday 7:00-10:00 peak -- 8.4 minutes on average from register to handoff across Q2 2026 -- producing walk-aways, comped drinks, remakes, and peak-end overtime the COPQ worksheet priced at $4,021 for the quarter ($16,084/yr on the charter, Q2 actuals x 4). Customers told us the line plainly: more than five minutes and they go to the vending machine. The project was chartered to fix the wait without breaking what works: drink quality (remake rate) and labor hours ride along as guardrail metrics.

The measured baseline (120 orders, 10 mornings, July 2026, run through the live stats engine): mean 8.41 minutes, sd 1.04, and STABLE -- zero control-chart signals. That stability is the finding: nothing special was going wrong on bad mornings; the process was built to produce an 8.4-minute wait. Against the customer's 5.0-minute line it was not capable -- Cpk -1.14, every one of the 120 sampled orders over the line -- so the fix had to remove common causes from the process itself, not chase bad days.

Reduce average order-to-handoff time during the weekday 7:00-10:00 peak from 8.4 to 5.0 minutes by October 31, 2026 -- a 3.41-minute gap against the measured 8.41 baseline -- while the remake rate holds no worse than Q2's 3.6 per 100 orders and barista labor hours do not grow. The 5.0-minute target is the customer's own walk-away line, not a number we liked.

The delay tally named the vital few at exactly 80%: the drink-queue pileup ahead of the single espresso station (22 of 40 tallies, 55% -- a cup waits a median 4.5 of the 8.4 minutes before its shot starts) and grinder rework re-pulls (10 of 40, 25%, ~2 minutes each). The 5-Why chain under the pileup ran three deep to an Improve-ready root: one machine head, batch sizes locked to one drink at a time. Two suspects were ruled out with the evidence kept on the board (register hardware -- a 0.8-minute step; measurement clock skew -- the check passed at 8.94%), and the daypart/staffing question tested real but minor (late mornings 0.45 min slower, both windows 3+ minutes past the promise), so staffing shape stayed honestly under investigation rather than verified.

Three candidate fixes, each linked to a verified cause, scored on declared criteria (gap impact 0.5, effort 0.25, cost 0.25 -- weights set before scores): (1) batch milk steaming + marked-cup sequencing, a $40 method change attacking the one-head batching root, weighted total 4.25; (2) a backup grinder + dose dial-in routine attacking rework, 3.5; (3) a second machine head, 3.0 -- the highest gap-impact score on the board (5) and still last on cost and effort ($9-14k plus install weeks against a $40 method change). It stayed ranked as the known escalation, not rejected. The list ran as a queue: one change piloted at a time, in rank order -- a draft pilot bundling two changes was refused by the engine with EXIT-10 named, and the second change waited its turn.

Round 1 (batch steaming + sequencing, threshold declared 7.0 before the pilot): the window came in at 6.20 min -- threshold met, Welch t = 17.87, p = 2.2e-45, d = 2.31 -- recovering 2.21 of the 3.41-minute gap (64.8%) with 1.20 remaining, so the loop took the next-ranked cause instead of stopping. Round 2 (grinder dial-in + standby swap, threshold 5.5): 4.90 min -- threshold met, and the cumulative gap check against the July baseline reads GOAL MET (remaining -0.10). Two honest riders travel with that result, exactly as the proof printed them. First, fall semester began mid-project: round 2 ran under ~15% more demand than the baseline windows, a declared confound that weakens the proof -- though its direction (more load, longer queues) could only mask improvement, not fake it. Second, the mean promise is met but the every-order promise is not: the improved process is stable at 4.90 with Cpk 0.05 against the 5.0 line -- the engine's model puts ~43.9% of orders over five minutes (46 of the 120 sampled orders were). Guardrails both improved: remakes 3.6 to 2.3 per 100, labor hours 8.65 to 8.1 per morning shift.

The improved state is held by an armed I-MR chart with limits frozen from the round-2 window (center 4.90, limits 3.03 / 6.77 -- the customer's 5.0 stays a spec line, never a control limit) and a control plan with named owners who accepted: Priya Shah on the daily handoff entries and the twice-weekly method spot-check, Marcus Webb on the weekly remake roll-up. Each monitored item has an investigate-then-respond OCAP that starts with the two changed methods -- did the batch/sequencing or the grinder dial-in lapse? -- before anyone touches a knob. All four staff are trained on the T-24 SOP with observed-demonstration sign-offs. Two weekly check-ins have come due so far; both were answered on time and both passed against the frozen band. The chart has been armed and quiet since the freeze: zero signals.

What the record teaches, including what went wrong: our first charter draft named the fix instead of the problem and had to be rewritten when the prescore flagged its solution language -- left standing, it would have chartered a $12k machine before the $40 method change got a look. The daypart study we expected to carry the staffing story came back real but minor -- a dead end that saved a pointless schedule reshuffle. And the close is deliberately modest: partial recovery per round was the plan working, not failing -- 64.8% then the remainder -- while the capability number (Cpk 0.05) keeps the team honest that averaging under five minutes is not the same promise as EVERY order under five.

realized_benefits.annualized_projection_basis: 4-week realized recovery x 13: (1,237.23 - 252.95) = 984.28 per four-week window, x 13 windows/yr = 12,795.64 -- proportional COPQ recovery carried forward, equivalently the quarter's proportional recovery (984.28 x 13/4 = 3,198.91) x 4 quarters. Assumes semester demand and the window's improved rates hold year-round; the before side of the delta is itself the Q2 baseline pro-rated to the same 4 weeks (4,021 x 4/13 = 1,237.23), so this projects the measured recovery, never the charter's original 16,084.
